Sinking of the SS United States Pushed a Day Earlier, Goodbye Ceremony Cancelled
10 photos
Photo: Okaloosa Board of County Commissioners/Facebook
The official ending of SS United States isn’t a quiet one. After the Okaloosa Board of County Commissioners’ official announcement in late October that the iconic ship would be sunk Thursday, on November 12, first a last-effort legal battle tried to halt the process altogether, then weather predictions brought another bump in the road. The date has now officially changed to Wednesday, November 11, but the planned farewell ceremony is definitively cancelled.
The sinking of the SS United States is one of the saddest events this year for historic ship aficionados in the US. Even if Okaloosa officials have tried to paint this as a happy event, given that the ship will become what is considered to be the largest artificial reef in the world, sure to attract lots of divers and tourists to Destin, Florida, everyone can feel the heaviness of this historic event that feels tragic.
A comment on the Okaloosa Board’s official Facebook page stated that “Even in death, she looks more powerful than ships today,” and another echoed that sentiment by adding that “There will never be another beautiful lady such as this”, yet people are still debating on whether this was the right decision for SS United States.
The “preservationist” side believes that the iconic ocean liner should have been saved, refitted, and turned into an active commercial ship, or at least a museum. On the other side, officials have argued that the ship was beyond repair and that trying to hold on to it would be far too costly; instead, sinking it in order to become a man-made reef would provide benefits for the marine environment and for the community, while still preserving the ship’s memory.
Last Monday, the SS United States Preservation Foundation, a small non-profit that was very active in trying to save the ship from reefing, filed a law suit trying to stop the process, and a motion seeking a temporary restraining order. The law suit argued that the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers hadn’t properly addressed the potential environmental impact, and historic preservation concerns were also added.
However, the final decision of a Florida federal judge denied these requests, allowing Okaloosa officials to move forward with the planned sinking. That’s when, unexpectedly, weather conditions caused another turn of events. A controlled sinking is much more complex than it sounds, and highly weather-dependent.
According to Okaloosa County, because “unsafe weather conditions” are forecast for Thursday, the controlled sinking was moved a day earlier, which also happens to be Veterans Day, an added symbolism that many people seemed to appreciate. For the same reason, the sendoff ceremony that was supposed to take place a day before the sinking, was also cancelled.
Folks everywhere will still be able to watch the sinking live-streamed – the link for it will be shared officially on thessus.com, prior to the event. Yesterday, the ship has officially left Mobile, Alabama, headed toward Destin, Florida. The deployment is set to begin at 1 p.m. CST.
If no new obstacle shows up, the American ocean liner that broke the record as the fastest passenger ship to cross the Atlantic will be sunk forever , and turned into the world’s largest artificial reef.
